transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-12-14 15:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (VectorScale CTO), Carlos Ruiz (ML Infra Lead), Dana Lee (SRE)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand VectorScale's p95 latency targets for streaming responses, expected concurrent sessions, token/sec bursts, and which deployment modes (hosted vs dedicated vs private) are on the table. Goal: scope a pilot that proves p95 streaming <= 250ms for short prompts and sustained throughput at 3k tokens/sec aggregate for typical nightly jobs, with fallsbacks.

Topics covered:
- p95 targets and how they measure today
- streaming vs batch token throughput
- concurrency and session counts (web chat + async jobs)
- hosted vs dedicated vs private constraints (data residency, KMS, SSO)
- benchmark plan and artifacts
- security questionnaires and SOC2 questions

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): alright everyone thanks for joining, i'm ethan from Redwood inference, i'll kick us off. quick roll call?
[00:09] Priya (VectorScale): priya here, carlos and dana are with me.
[00:13] Carlos (VectorScale): hey all.
[00:15] Maya (Redwood SE): maya here, i'll handle the performance bits.
[00:18] Dana (VectorScale): dana, ops.

[00:30] Ethan: cool, context — VectorScale is building an embeddable analytics assistant, right? multi-tenant, lots of short interactive sessions plus some overnight batch summarization jobs?
[00:41] Priya: yea that's it. the interactive sessions are chatty, average 40 tokens in prompt and 120 tokens generated per turn, users expect snappy streaming. the overnight jobs are heavy token throughput, we want consistent cost.

[01:05] Maya: can you share p95 expectations for interactive? is this 200ms, 500ms, 1 second?
[01:12] Priya: target is 200 to 300ms p95 for the streamed first token for short responses, end-to-end maybe 400 for full generation, but first token priority.

[01:28] Carlos: also concurrency, peak is about 1,800 concurrent sessions for EU region, global peak 3k. but those are pages/views not all generating simultaneously, we estimate 900 concurrent active generations at peak.

[01:45] Dana: and for batch, we have spikes to 150k tokens/sec during nightly ETL windows but it's transient over 15 minutes.

[02:05] Maya: ok great detail. a couple of clarifying things — when you say streaming p95 200-300ms, is that measured from request arrival to first byte out to the client or to full decoded token? also do you have TLS termination in your infra or via our hosted endpoint?
[02:20] Priya: first byte to client, user-perceived latency. TLS termination is at our edge right now but for pilot we can use Redwood hosted TLS.

[02:40] Ethan: great. high level on deployment preferences? are you leaning hosted for speed to production, or do you need dedicated/reserved capacity or private VPC/on-prem for compliance?
[02:52] Priya: we prefer hosted initially to iterate, but enterprise customers will require VPC/private options with KMS integration for keying. so both hosted then dedicated/private for enterprise rollout.

[03:10] Carlos: security row — SOC2 is mandatory, SAML SSO, audit logs, and customer data must be isolated per enterprise. encryption at rest with our KMS is needed for private.

[03:28] Maya: Redwood supports SOC2, SSO, per-tenant audit logging and KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. for Dedicated we can offer reserves with data isolation and optional KMS setup.

[03:45] Priya: good. on perf, curious about batching and KV cache — can you talk about streaming with prefix KV cache and how that impacts p95? sometimes caches increase tail latency if cold.

[04:03] Maya: yeah good point. we do prefix and KV cache; for interactive streaming we prioritize low tail latency by doing small continuous batching and using per-session KV to avoid re-computation. cold KV cache misses will add a few ms to tens of ms depending on model and sequence length — but we tune kernel selection and memory placement for predictable tails.

[04:26] Carlos: what about model size? our plan is to run two model families, a 13B quantized and a 70B quantized variant for higher quality with fallback. how does that change throughput and p95?

[04:40] Maya: 13B quantized will get much higher tokens/sec and lower latency — p95 typically below 200ms for short streams on a well-optimized GPU setup. 70B even quantized has higher memory pressure and can push p95 up, especially at high concurrency. we use routing policies to send latency-sensitive traffic to smaller models and cost-tolerant to larger ones.

[05:10] Ethan: for the pilot we usually propose a small matrix: hosted with 13B at expected concurrency, plus a dedicated run with mixed 13B/70B to measure fallback and routing. we can also test quantization modes and batching windows.

[05:25] Priya: sounds good. about benchmarking — what artifacts do you need from us?

[05:31] Maya: prompt set, distribution of prompt lengths, expected per-session token counts, concurrency profile over time, and whether streaming first-byte or full response is critical. also network path — are you testing from EU region to EU hosted endpoints?

[05:46] Priya: yes region matters — started EU first. we'll provide traffic traces and the actual prompt set.

[06:00] Dana: on measurement, do you instrument p95 at the SDK client side or use your console metrics? we need safeguards for synthetic tests vs real-world variance.

[06:10] Maya: both — we surface token-level latency in console and can provide raw trace exports. for the pilot we'll recommend client-side measurement to capture user perceived p95 and compare to server SLOs.

[06:24] Carlos: any known gotchas with TLS and streaming? our infra multiplies proxies.

[06:29] Maya: proxies add head-of-line issues sometimes — keep idle timeouts high and avoid double buffering, we can share best-practice configs. also advise on chunk size for streaming to reduce latency spikes.

[06:45] Priya: what about cost implications — if we route to dedicated smaller models aggressively, that's cost savings but might reduce quality. our product team will want tradeoff numbers.

[06:56] Ethan: we'll include cost-per-1M tokens for each model variant and an example of routing policy that prioritizes latency for interactive sessions. dedicated reserved capacity pricing will show unit economics at scale.

[07:12] Carlos: do you support per-request quantize setting or is quantization baked per model?

[07:17] Maya: quantization profiles are model builds — you can host multiple quantized variants and we route between them. changing quantization per request isn't typical.

[07:28] Priya: good to know. on fallback, how fast can you switch from hosted to dedicated or to smaller model if load spikes?

[07:36] Ethan: routing policies can detect capacity pressure and shift to compatible variants within seconds; we recommend canary and circuit-breaker settings so there's graceful degradation.

[07:50] Dana: and observability — can you surface token-level cost in traces?

[07:54] Maya: yes per-request token breakdown, and we can annotate traces with model variant and kernel selection for post-mortem.

[08:05] Priya: competitors — we've run tests with OpenAI and Anthropic; noticed OpenAI was smoother for small prompt first-byte but cost was higher at scale. how do you compare?

[08:18] Ethan: we aim to sit between in quality/cost — with more control over deployment and predictable unit economics. we'll include comparative figures but caveat that workloads vary.

[08:33] Carlos: on the pilot, can you support a reproducible token/sec stress harness? we want to run controlled spike tests that mimic our ETL bursts.

[08:42] Maya: yes we have a stress harness. for streaming we simulate concurrent sessions with realistic jitter and payloads. we'll collaborate on an artifact that you can run or let us run in our test environment with your telemetry.

[09:00] Priya: great. one other question — for private deployments we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs forwarded into our SIEM. is that supported?

[09:10] Maya: yes Private supports KMS and HSM integrations, and logs can be forwarded via syslog or S3 exports for ingestion into your SIEM. we'll send our security integration guide.

[09:22] Ethan: perfect. let's quickly map out the pilot phases so expectations are clear.

[09:29] Maya: phase one — hosted quickstart: run 13B quantized in hosted for 2 weeks with lowered latency SLOs, run synthetic stream tests and compare client-side p95. phase two — dedicated/reserved run with traffic shaping to measure cost & regionized throughput. phase three — private/VPC test with KMS for enterprise tenant.

[09:54] Priya: timeline checks out. we'd want phase one in December to validate before enterprise sales push in January.

[10:03] Carlos: what SLOs should we set for the pilot to consider it successful?

[10:08] Ethan: recommended success criteria: first-byte streaming p95 <= 300ms for 95% of client-side synthetic runs at 900 concurrent active generations, and sustained aggregate tokens/sec >= 3k during non-batch windows; batch windows measured for short 15-minute spikes should sustain 100k-150k tokens/sec without service degradation in dedicated runs.

[10:36] Dana: that seems reasonable. also want an SLA for failover and fallback behavior documented.

[10:41] Maya: we'll include canary/fallback docs and a runbook.

[10:48] Priya: ok do you need anything else from us today?

[10:52] Maya: just the prompt set and traffic profile, and ideally a short list of customers with strict residency so we can prioritize region tests.

[11:02] Priya: we'll send those.

[11:05] Ethan: i'll send the pricing and next steps. maya will send benchmark plan. propose next meeting 2027-12-22 to kick off pilot.

[11:16] Carlos: noted. also please attach the security integrations doc and SOC2 attestation.

[11:22] Ethan: will do.

[11:30] Priya: thanks everyone.

[47:30] End of call — informal wrap up chatter and off-topic scheduling.
